summary: In this episode of the Lord of Spirits, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young explore the concept of Doomsday, the final judgment, and the end of days. They begin by discussing the biblical and historical origins of the phrase 'end of days,' noting that while the exact phrase does not appear in the Bible, the concept is derived from the creation narrative and the promise of a final day. They emphasize that the idea of history having a beginning and an end is a biblical creation, contrasting it with cyclical views of time in the ancient world. The hosts then delve into the nature of judgment, defining justice as the state of everything being in its proper order, and explain that the final judgment is about restoring that order. They use agricultural metaphors from the Gospels, such as the parable of the weeds and the vine and branches, to illustrate two types of judgment: macrocosmic (the final separation of wheat and tares) and microcosmic (pruning for correction and growth). They also discuss the Day of the Lord in the Old Testament, showing how it refers to historical judgments on nations like Babylon and Egypt, and how these events are participations in the final judgment. The second half focuses on the New Testament teaching that all people will be judged according to their works, citing passages from Matthew, Romans, 2 Corinthians, 1 Peter, Colossians, and Revelation. They address the common objection that this contradicts salvation by faith, clarifying that while salvation is a gift of God's grace, the judgment is based on the works that flow from faith, which are actually God's works performed through us. They connect this to the principle of iconography, arguing that honoring the image of God in others is honoring Christ, and that this principle is foundational to Christian ethics and theology. In the final half, they explore the connection between the bodily resurrection and the final judgment, showing that the resurrection is necessary for justice to be fully realized, as individuals must be raised in their bodies to receive vindication or condemnation. They trace this belief to Old Testament texts like Job, Isaiah, and Daniel, and explain how the resurrection of Christ is seen as his vindication and the basis for our justification. They conclude with an exhortation to live faithfully, doing the works of God, so that we may be vindicated at the last judgment and hear 'well done, good and faithful servant.'

entities.title: Father Andrew Stephen Damick
entities.summary: One of the hosts of the Lord of Spirits podcast, an Orthodox Christian priest.

entities.title: Father Stephen De Young
entities.summary: One of the hosts of the Lord of Spirits podcast, an Orthodox Christian priest.

entities.title: Babylon
entities.summary: An ancient city and empire often used in the Bible as a symbol of pride and opposition to God. The hosts discuss the Day of the Lord coming upon Babylon.

entities.title: Job
entities.summary: A righteous man in the Old Testament who suffered greatly and expressed hope in the bodily resurrection and vindication.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The central figure of Christianity, whose death and resurrection are discussed in relation to judgment and vindication.

entities.title: Saint Paul
entities.summary: An apostle whose writings emphasize judgment according to works and the resurrection as vindication.

entities.title: Saint Peter
entities.summary: An apostle who preached the resurrection of Christ as his vindication.

entities.title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria
entities.summary: A Church Father who interpreted 2 Corinthians 5:21 as referring to Christ as a sin offering.

entities.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
entities.summary: A civil rights leader quoted for the idea that the arc of history bends toward justice.

entities.title: Pharisees
entities.summary: A Jewish sect that believed in the bodily resurrection, as opposed to the Sadducees.

entities.title: Sadducees
entities.summary: A Jewish sect that did not believe in the bodily resurrection, and only considered the Torah as authoritative.

entities.title: William the Conqueror
entities.summary: The Norman king who commissioned the Domesday Book, which is related to the etymology of 'doomsday'.

concepts.title: End of Days
concepts.summary: The concept of the end of days refers to the final period of history leading up to the last judgment. While the exact phrase does not appear in the Bible, it is derived from the creation narrative and the promise of a final day. The hosts discuss its origins in Second Temple Jewish literature and its use in Christian theology.

concepts.title: Day of the Lord
concepts.summary: A biblical term for a time of divine judgment, often described with apocalyptic imagery. The hosts explain that it can refer to historical judgments on nations as well as the final judgment, and that it is a day of both destruction and vindication.

concepts.title: Justice as Order
concepts.summary: The biblical concept of justice (mishpat) is defined as the state of everything being in its proper place and functioning correctly. This understanding underlies the idea of judgment as the restoration of order in creation.

concepts.title: Macrocosmic Judgment
concepts.summary: The final judgment of the whole world, as depicted in the parable of the weeds, where the righteous and wicked are separated at the end of the age.

concepts.title: Microcosmic Judgment
concepts.summary: The ongoing judgment of individuals through correction and discipline, as illustrated by the pruning of vines. This type of judgment is aimed at repentance and growth in righteousness.

concepts.title: Judgment by Works
concepts.summary: The consistent biblical teaching that all people will be judged according to their deeds, both good and evil. This is not opposed to salvation by grace but is the basis for the final assessment of one's life.

concepts.title: Theosis
concepts.summary: The process of becoming like God, often described as participating in the divine nature. The hosts connect this to the resurrection and the final judgment, noting that the righteous will shine like stars.

concepts.title: Bodily Resurrection
concepts.summary: The belief that the dead will be raised in their physical bodies at the last day. This is essential for justice, as individuals must be resurrected to receive vindication or condemnation for their deeds.

concepts.title: Works Righteousness
concepts.summary: The idea that one can earn salvation through good deeds. The hosts clarify that while judgment is according to works, salvation is not earned; rather, the works are God's works performed through us.

concepts.title: Iconoclasm
concepts.summary: The rejection of icons and the principle that honor given to an image passes to the prototype. The hosts argue that this principle is foundational to Christian ethics and theology, and that iconoclasm undermines the doctrine of the Trinity and Christology.

claims.text: The idea that history has a beginning and an end is a biblical creation, contrasting with cyclical views of time in the ancient world.
Objective justice is impossible without an existing order that defines what is just; the biblical concept of justice is tied to the order of creation.
Every place in Scripture that discusses the basis for the final judgment says that people are judged according to their works, not their beliefs.
Salvation is by works in the sense of theurgy—God's works performed through us—not by our own independent merits.
The bodily resurrection is necessary for justice because individuals must be raised in their bodies to receive vindication or condemnation for their deeds.
The resurrection of Christ is his vindication as the righteous one, and it is the basis for our justification.
The principle that honor given to an image passes to the prototype is foundational to the doctrine of the Trinity; iconoclasm undermines it.
